title: When a landing page should be a product screen
metaTitle: Show the product on the landing page
excerpt: If the product is the argument, show the product. A landing page of benefits with no screen asks the buyer to imagine the thing you could have put in front of them.
alt: A dim desk with an iMac showing a code editor beside a portfolio page, a second monitor with a mountain wallpaper, and a lit lamp, the product on the screen instead of a list of benefits.
caption: The product on the screen, a lamp, and a second monitor. If the product is the argument, show it. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should a landing page show the product?
faqs.answer: When a buyer cannot judge the offer without seeing the interface. Put a real screen, with believable data and the actual verb on the button, in the first view or one short scroll from it. Benefits should point at something in that frame.

faqs.question: When should you avoid a product screenshot?
faqs.answer: When you sell a service, a place, or an object, and a fake dashboard would be a category error. Also skip a concept film of features you have not shipped. A prototype is fair only if it is the workflow you will actually release, and you label it as a prototype.

faqs.question: What should the screenshot contain?
faqs.answer: A believable state, cropped so the decision is readable on a phone. Caption it with a claim the picture supports. Update the image when the workflow changes, because a stale screen teaches the buyer a product you no longer have.

markdown:
If the product is the argument, the landing page should show the product. A screen, with real labels, doing the job the buyer came to judge. A product led landing page that lists benefits and never shows the interface asks the buyer to imagine the thing you could have put in front of them.

Put the screen in the first view, or one short scroll from it. The sentence can name the job. The picture has to prove the sentence. Benefits can sit beside the screen. They cannot replace it.

## When the screen is the proof

Show the product when a buyer cannot evaluate you any other way. Software is the usual case. A workflow tool, a dashboard, a booking system, a catalog manager. The buyer has been disappointed by adjectives before. "Simple," "powerful," and "all-in-one" are claims. A screen is evidence.

Show it when the sale happens before a sales call, or when the call starts with "can you just show me?" If your best salesperson shares their screen in the first five minutes, the page should have done that already. You are saving the buyer a meeting, or making the meeting about their data instead of your tour.

Show it when the difference between you and the alternative is structural. A scanable list versus a pile of menus. A single primary action versus a toolbar of equal buttons. Trade Moai is a public Hanabi example of an interface organized so a person can scan. Got Next and Leadly are public examples of focused product UI. The marketing lesson from those kinds of interfaces is the same. The crop should teach the hierarchy. A glow around a logo does not.

You can still write a sentence. The sentence says who the screen is for and what just happened in it. "A warehouse lead sees today's exceptions, and nothing else, until those are cleared." Then the reader looks at the screen and checks whether that sentence is true. That is a fair test. A page that cannot pass it is not ready.

## What to put in the frame

Use a real state. A believable name, a believable number, a task half finished. Lorem and "Acme" and a perfect empty chart tell the buyer this is a costume. If the data must be fake, make it specific enough that a practitioner would nod. One awkward detail, a long customer name, a zero in a column, does more than a stock illustration.

Show the action. The button with the verb you actually use. The row a person would click. If the product's point is a sequence, two frames beat a single heroic crop: before the decision, and after. Do not show six frames. Two is a proof. Six is a manual, and manuals belong in the product or in a guide.

Crop to the decision. Include enough chrome that the screen is recognizable as your product, and cut the parts that do not serve the sentence. A full desktop at 40 percent scale is unreadable on a phone. A tight crop of the one control, with a caption, is honest. On a phone, consider a single column of the real mobile UI if that is how the job is done. Many products are judged on a laptop and used on a phone. Show the one the buyer will be held to.

Write the caption as a claim a skeptic can check. "Exceptions are sorted by age, not by which account shouted last." If the screen does not show that, change the screen or change the caption. Do not let marketing words float beside a UI that contradicts them.

Hanabi designs these frames in Figma, and checks them in the browser, because type that looks fine in a mock often fails at the size the landing page actually renders. The build is the same stack as the rest of the site: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind. Motion can walk someone through a sequence if it earns it, with a reduced-motion path that still shows the end state. The end state matters more than the tour. A person who does not wait for the animation must still see the product.

## Benefits, arranged around the screen

A benefit earns its place by pointing at something in the frame. "See the exception without opening a ticket" next to the row that is the exception. A benefit that could sit on a competitor's site, with no anchor in the picture, is a slogan. Move it down or cut it.

Three anchored benefits are enough under the first screen. Each one: a verb, the object, and the person. Skip the icon set that restates the same idea in a circle. If you cannot draw the benefit in the product, you may be selling a service, not a screen. That is a legitimate business. It wants a different page, with the work and the constraint, not a fake UI.

Logos of customers can sit below, after the screen has done its work. A logo row above the fold, with the product pushed down, repeats the partner-page mistake: recognition instead of a sentence. One sentence from a real user is stronger than twelve marks, and only if you have permission and the sentence is true. Do not invent a quote to fill the gap. Leave the gap and show the screen.

Price, or the shape of the price, can live on this page if the buyer needs it to stay. It should not shove the screen below a comparison table. The screen is why the table might be worth reading. Link to a pricing page if the table is long. Keep one action here: start a trial, book a demo, or open the product. Pick the one that matches how you actually sell.

## When a landing page should stay a landing page

Stay with words and proof, and do not fake a product, when the thing you sell is a service, a place, or an object. A studio, a workshop, a manufacturer, a local shop. Down the Cove is an ecommerce migration and redesign. The "screen" there is the shop a person can buy from, which is worth showing. Thomas Bewick is an editorial heritage site. The proof is the reading experience, which is also worth showing. Wabisabi and Ballarat Box Sports are brands where the object or the community is the argument. A pretend dashboard would be a category error.

Stay with a landing page when the product is too early to show without lying. A clickable prototype of a real workflow can stand in, labeled as a prototype, if the flow is the one you will ship. A concept film of features you might build is an ad. Label it as a direction, or do not use it as proof. Buyers who feel misled do not become patient later.

Stay with a landing page when the audience on this URL is not a user. An investor, a recruit, a journalist. They may need the screen eventually. They do not need it disguised as the homepage for buyers. Give them their path. Keep the buyer's first screen pointed at the product.

If you have three audiences, the screen still belongs to the audience that pays. The others get a labeled path. A homepage that tries to demo three products in one hero will demo none of them at a readable size.

## Making the screen true in production

The landing page and the product should share type, color, and verbs. If the marketing button says "Start free" and the product button says "Create workspace," pick one. The drift looks small in two files and large to the person who just clicked.

Use a real build for the screenshot, or a carefully exported frame from the same components. A screenshot from a branch nobody will ship becomes false on launch day. Assign someone to update the image when the workflow changes. A stale screen is worse than no screen, because it teaches the buyer a product you no longer have.

Check the page the way you check the product. On a phone. With a long label. With reduced motion. web.dev's threshold for cumulative layout shift, 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile, is easy to miss when a large product image arrives late and pushes the button. Reserve the space. The button should not jump.

Alt text should describe the screen, including the job it shows, for someone who cannot see it. "Dashboard" is not a description. "A list of overdue orders, oldest at the top, with one primary action to assign them" is a description. The WCAG principles, starting with perceivable, apply to the marketing page as much as to the app. The landing page is not exempt because it is pretty.

## What you ask the buyer to do next

One action. If the product can be tried, let them try the same job the screen just showed. Dropping them into an empty account with no path is a bait and switch made of good intentions. Seed the trial with the example, or walk the first run until the screen they saw is the screen they have.

If the product cannot be tried without a conversation, the action is a call, and the page should say what the call is for. "Bring one workflow. We will put it in the product." That sets a standard. A form that says "Tell us about your needs" throws away the specificity you just earned.

A salesperson who sends a single feature, rather than this whole homepage, needs a page that is even tighter. One feature, the job it finishes, a picture, and who it is for. The piece on [writing a feature page a salesperson can send](/blog/writing-a-feature-page-a-salesperson-can-send) is the next read if your product is too wide for one screen to carry.

To see product-shaped work treated as proof, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The standard to steal is simple. If the product is the argument, it is in the picture, at a size a skeptic can read.
